answers.answer: The analogue is section 3(1) of the Misrepresentation Ordinance (Cap. 284). It is in materially identical terms to s.2(1) of the English Misrepresentation Act 1967: where a person has entered into a contract after a misrepresentation made to him by another party and has suffered loss, the representor is liable in damages as though the representation had been made fraudulently, unless he proves he had reasonable ground to believe, and did believe up to the time the contract was made, that the facts represented were true. The numbering runs one ahead of the English Act throughout, so Cap. 284 s.3(2) corresponds to English s.2(2) (damages in lieu of rescission) and Cap. 284 s.4 corresponds to English s.3 (control of exclusion clauses).

Section 4 of the Misrepresentation Ordinance (Cap. 284) is the gateway: a contract term that would exclude or restrict liability for a pre-contractual misrepresentation, or restrict a remedy for it, is of no effect except in so far as it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness. Cap. 284 s.4 does not define that requirement itself; it imports the reasonableness test from the Control of Exemption Clauses Ordinance (Cap. 71), which is stated in s.3 of Cap. 71 and elaborated by the guidelines in Schedule 2 to that Ordinance. The burden of proving that the clause satisfies the test lies on the party seeking to rely on it. This mirrors the English pairing of s.3 of the Misrepresentation Act 1967 with s.11(1) of UCTA 1977.

Yes. The contractual estoppel doctrine of Peekay Intermark Ltd v Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd [2006] EWCA Civ 386 and Springwell Navigation Corp v JP Morgan Chase Bank [2010] EWCA Civ 1221 has been received into Hong Kong law and applied repeatedly, notably in the private-banking mis-selling litigation (at first instance, e.g. DBS Bank (Hong Kong) Ltd v San-Hot HK Industrial Co Ltd (Bharwaney J) and Li Kwok Heem John v Standard Chartered International (Excelsior) Ltd [2016] 1 HKLRD 152), and at appellate level in Kwok Wai Hing Selina v HSBC Private Bank (Suisse) SA and in Chang Pui Yin v Bank of Singapore Ltd [2017] 4 HKLRD 458. The adoption therefore currently rests at Court of Appeal level: the Court of Final Appeal has not, so far as I am aware, pronounced on the doctrine, so it has not been settled at the apex of the hierarchy. I am confident about the Court of Appeal level and about Chang Pui Yin; I am less certain of the precise report citation for Kwok Wai Hing Selina.

Chang Pui Yin v Bank of Singapore Ltd [2017] 4 HKLRD 458 (Court of Appeal; CACV 194/2016, Kwan JA). The two bases were, first, characterisation: the non-reliance and no-advice provisions in the bank's standard documentation were held to operate in substance as clauses excluding or restricting liability rather than as true 'basis' clauses defining the dealing, so they were caught by the statutory controls - s.4 of the Misrepresentation Ordinance (Cap. 284) for misrepresentation and the negligence provisions of the Control of Exemption Clauses Ordinance (Cap. 71). Second, applying the reasonableness test, the clauses failed it on the facts: the customers were unsophisticated, had limited command of the English-language standard forms, the terms were not negotiated, and the bank knew that they were in fact relying on its relationship manager's advice and had mis-recorded their risk profile. The effect is that contractual estoppel is accepted in principle in Hong Kong but cannot be used to sidestep the statutory reasonableness control against an unsophisticated customer. I am confident of the case and of the reasonableness-failure basis; the 'exclusion rather than basis clause' characterisation is my recollection of the first basis and I flag slight uncertainty on how precisely the Court framed it.

I am not able to state this reliably from memory. My recollection is that Green Park Properties Ltd v Dorku Ltd (2001) 4 HKCFAR 448 is a Court of Final Appeal decision arising out of a Hong Kong property sale in which the exclusion / 'no representation' provision failed to protect the vendor, and that the reasoning turned on the statutory control in s.4 of the Misrepresentation Ordinance (Cap. 284) read with the Control of Exemption Clauses Ordinance (Cap. 71) - the party relying on the clause bearing, and not discharging, the burden of proving reasonableness. I cannot confirm that reasoning, and I may be conflating it with other authority; I would treat the point as unverified rather than rely on it. If the precise ratio matters, the report should be checked.

Neither is binding. By Articles 8 and 18 of the Basic Law the common law previously in force in Hong Kong was maintained after 1 July 1997, and Article 84 permits Hong Kong courts to refer to precedents of other common law jurisdictions - which is the status such decisions now have. (a) A pre-1997 House of Lords decision is not, and strictly never was, binding in Hong Kong (final appeals lay to the Privy Council, not the House of Lords), but pre-handover English decisions that formed part of the common law as it stood in 1997 are treated as very highly persuasive and are ordinarily followed. (b) A post-1997 UK Supreme Court decision is of persuasive weight only, to be weighed on its reasoning and its fit with Hong Kong conditions. The Court of Final Appeal authority usually cited on the status of pre-handover precedent and the CFA's freedom to depart from it is Solicitor (24/07) v Law Society of Hong Kong (2008) 11 HKCFAR 117; I am confident about the constitutional propositions but only moderately confident that this is the decision the question has in mind.

I am not aware of any Hong Kong decision - appellate or otherwise - that squarely decides whether damages under s.3(1) of Cap. 284 are assessed on the deceit measure adopted in Royscot Trust Ltd v Rogerson [1991] 2 QB 297. Because the wording of s.3(1) is identical to the English s.2(1) ('as if the representation had been made fraudulently'), the Royscot reading is generally assumed in Hong Kong practice and texts to apply, and I believe it has been proceeded on rather than argued at first instance, but that is an assumption rather than a holding. On what I have, the honest answer is that the point is not established by Hong Kong authority, and I cannot name a case deciding it.

I cannot answer this with confidence. My recollection of Shine Grace Investment Ltd v Citibank NA [2018] HKCFI 1737 is that it was a long CFI trial arising from leveraged derivative/accumulator positions and the forced close-out of the plaintiff's portfolio in the 2008 crisis, and that the misrepresentation case failed at least in part because the court found the individual who was the plaintiff's controlling mind was an experienced investor who made her own decisions and did not in fact rely on the matters alleged - inducement therefore not being made out on the evidence. I am not confident of that detail and cannot vouch for the precise reasoning or the findings on which it rested; the judgment should be checked before this is relied on.

Advising in 2012, the position was unsettled but had moved decisively in favour of enforceability. Following Peekay Intermark Ltd v Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd [2006] EWCA Civ 386 and Springwell Navigation Corp v JP Morgan Chase Bank [2010] EWCA Civ 1221, and the analysis of Christopher Clarke J in Raiffeisen Zentralbank Osterreich AG v Royal Bank of Scotland plc [2010] EWHC 1392 (Comm), the accepted distinction was between a clause that excludes liability for a representation actually made (caught by s.3 of the Misrepresentation Act 1967) and a 'basis' clause that defines the parties' dealing so that no representation is made at all - the latter falling outside s.3 and instead giving rise to a contractual estoppel. The correct advice in 2012 was therefore that a carefully drafted non-reliance clause would probably escape s.3, but with a live risk the other way, since Cremdean Properties Ltd v Nash (1977) 244 EG 547, Government of Zanzibar v British Aerospace (Lancaster House) Ltd [2000] 1 WLR 2333 and first-instance decisions such as Foodco UK LLP v Henry Boot Developments Ltd [2010] EWHC 358 (Ch) pointed to substance over form. That risk crystallised later, in First Tower Trustees Ltd v CDS (Superstores International) Ltd [2018] EWCA Civ 1396.

In 2014 the orthodox rule was that the representation had to be 'actively present to the mind' of the representee and to be a real and substantial (not necessarily the sole) inducing cause: Smith v Chadwick (1884) 9 App Cas 187; Edgington v Fitzmaurice (1885) 29 Ch D 459. On that footing mere suspicion of falsity did not preclude inducement, though it was arguable - and not clearly resolved - that a representee who positively disbelieved or knew the statement to be false could not be induced. The Court of Appeal then held in Hayward v Zurich Insurance Co plc [2015] EWCA Civ 327 that an insurer who suspected and had pleaded fraud could not establish inducement, which tightened the law. The Supreme Court reversed in Hayward v Zurich Insurance Co plc [2016] UKSC 48, [2017] AC 142, holding that belief in the truth of the representation is not a legal precondition of inducement; the question is one of fact and causation - whether the misrepresentation was a material cause of the representee's decision - so a suspicious but influenced representee can still succeed.

Where the misrepresentation is fraudulent the presumption of inducement is at its strongest and is very hard to displace: the burden lies on the fraudulent representor to prove that the representation played no part at all in the representee's decision, and it is not enough to show the representee might or would probably have contracted anyway. The leading modern statement is BV Nederlandse Industrie van Eiprodukten v Rembrandt Enterprises Inc [2019] EWCA Civ 596, [2020] QB 551 (Longmore LJ), which reviewed the authorities and held that in fraud the presumption can only be rebutted by showing the fraud had no effect on the representee's mind. It builds on Hayward v Zurich Insurance Co plc [2016] UKSC 48 and the older principle in Smith v Kay (1859) 7 HLC 750 and Redgrave v Hurd (1881) 20 Ch D 1 that a fraudster cannot complain that his victim was too ready to believe him.

Yes, formally. Royscot Trust Ltd v Rogerson [1991] 2 QB 297 is an undisturbed Court of Appeal decision and remains binding below the Supreme Court: damages under s.2(1) are assessed on the tortious deceit measure, so all loss flowing directly from the transaction is recoverable without a remoteness/foreseeability cut-off. The qualification is that its correctness has never been endorsed at the highest level and has been doubted - Lord Steyn expressly reserved the point in Smith New Court Securities Ltd v Scrimgeour Vickers (Asset Management) Ltd [1997] AC 254, and it has been heavily criticised academically - so it is vulnerable if the Supreme Court takes the point. A further qualification is that the 'fiction of fraud' is not carried through to every incident of deceit: contributory negligence can be pleaded against a s.2(1) claim where there is a concurrent common law duty of care (Gran Gelato Ltd v Richcliff (Group) Ltd [1992] Ch 560), whereas it is unavailable in deceit (Standard Chartered Bank v Pakistan National Shipping Corp (No 2) [2003] 1 AC 959).

Chronological order: (1) Peekay Intermark Ltd v Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd [2006] EWCA Civ 386 - toward enforcement: it established contractual estoppel, holding that parties may bind themselves to a contractual state of affairs (no reliance) even if untrue in fact. (2) Springwell Navigation Corp v JP Morgan Chase Bank [2010] EWCA Civ 1221 - further toward enforcement: it confirmed and broadened Peekay in the sophisticated-investor context and endorsed the 'basis clause' analysis by which such clauses escape s.3 of the Misrepresentation Act 1967 and UCTA. (3) Chang Pui Yin v Bank of Singapore Ltd [2017] 4 HKLRD 458 (Hong Kong Court of Appeal) - away from enforcement: while accepting contractual estoppel in principle, it held the bank's non-reliance and no-advice clauses were caught by the statutory controls (Cap. 284 s.4 and Cap. 71) and failed the reasonableness test against unsophisticated customers. (4) First Tower Trustees Ltd v CDS (Superstores International) Ltd [2018] EWCA Civ 1396, [2019] 1 WLR 637 - away from enforcement: it held that non-reliance clauses are subject to s.3 of the 1967 Act, substantially closing the 'basis clause' escape route, and found the clause unreasonable on the facts.

Singapore treats the so-called presumption of inducement not as a legal presumption that shifts the burden of proof, but as an inference of fact that a court may (not must) draw where the representation is material and of a kind objectively likely to induce. The legal burden of proving that he was in fact induced therefore remains on the representee throughout. The Court of Appeal authority is Broadley Construction Pte Ltd v Alacran Design Pte Ltd [2018] SGCA 25, [2018] 2 SLR 110 (Steven Chong JA), building on the elements set out in Panatron Pte Ltd v Lee Cheow Lee [2001] 3 SLR(R) 435. That differs from the usual English articulation (Redgrave v Hurd (1881) 20 Ch D 1; and in fraud, BV Nederlandse Industrie van Eiprodukten v Rembrandt Enterprises Inc [2019] EWCA Civ 596), where the presumption is described as casting onto the representor the burden of proving that the representee was not induced. I am confident on the Singapore characterisation; moderately confident on the exact Panatron citation.

No - Singapore has not committed itself to the Royscot 'fiction of fraud' measure. My recollection is that the Court of Appeal has noted the extensive criticism of Royscot Trust Ltd v Rogerson [1991] 2 QB 297 and expressly left open whether the deceit measure (with its absence of a remoteness cut-off) should govern damages under s.2(1) of the Singapore Misrepresentation Act, deciding the case before it on other grounds; the decision I associate with that reservation is RBC Properties Pte Ltd v Defu Furniture Pte Ltd [2014] SGCA 62, [2015] 1 SLR 997. I am only moderately confident of that citation and would flag it for checking. What I would state with confidence is the negative proposition: there is no Singapore Court of Appeal holding adopting Royscot, and the point should be treated as open.

The 1967 Act applied in Singapore first through general reception of English commercial law under s.5 of the Civil Law Act, and was then put on a clear footing by the Application of English Law Act 1993 (Cap. 7A), s.4 read with the First Schedule, which lists the English enactments that continue to apply in Singapore (with modifications) and excludes any other reception route. It was thereafter reprinted as a Singapore statute, the Misrepresentation Act (Cap. 390, 1994 Rev Ed), now the Misrepresentation Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed). As to differences, the changes I am aware of are adaptations rather than additions - notably that s.3 refers to the Singapore Unfair Contract Terms Act (Cap. 396, now the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (2020 Rev Ed)) rather than the UK Act, and the spent provision amending the (English) Sale of Goods Act 1893 is not carried over. I am not aware of a substantive provision in the Singapore version that has no counterpart in the English Act, but I hold that with only moderate confidence and would check the reprint if the point is load-bearing.

The question is open in Singapore. The Court of Appeal has flagged, without deciding, that non-reliance / contractual-estoppel clauses in standard-form banking documentation may be subject to statutory control under the Unfair Contract Terms Act (Cap. 396) and s.3 of the Misrepresentation Act, and has cautioned that contractual estoppel should not be allowed to defeat that control as a matter of course. The decision I associate with that flag is Als Memasa v UBS AG [2012] SGCA 43, [2012] 4 SLR 992 (Chan Sek Keong CJ), with related observations in Deutsche Bank AG v Chang Tse Wen [2013] SGCA 49, [2013] 4 SLR 886. I am confident that the point remains unresolved at Court of Appeal level in Singapore; I am moderately confident that Als Memasa is the decision the question has in mind.

I am not aware of any Hong Kong appellate authority drawing such a distinction, and I do not believe any exists. The half-truth rule - that a literally true statement may be actionable if what is left unsaid renders it misleading (Dimmock v Hallett (1866) LR 2 Ch App 21; Nottingham Patent Brick and Tile Co v Butler (1886) 16 QBD 778, applied in Hong Kong as part of the general law) - is a doctrine of general application. It is not subject-matter specific: the same test applies whether the contract is a share purchase agreement or a sale of land, and any apparent difference in outcome is a function of the factual context (what was said, and what an ordinary reader would take from it) rather than of a different legal rule. The honest answer is that no authority establishes the proposition the question posits.

The continuing-representation rule derives from With v O'Flanagan [1936] Ch 575 and Davies v London and Provincial Marine Insurance Co (1878) 8 Ch D 469: a representation of a continuing state of affairs is treated as repeated up to contract, so a representor who learns before contracting that his statement has become false must correct it, and failure to do so is an actionable misrepresentation. The leading Australian statement of the principle is Jones v Dumbrell [1981] VR 199 (Full Court of the Supreme Court of Victoria, Fullagar J), which is the citation ordinarily given in Australian texts. At High Court level, Krakowski v Eurolynx Properties Ltd (1995) 183 CLR 563 is the closest analogue: the vendor's later side arrangement with the tenant falsified the earlier representation about the lease, and non-disclosure of it was held actionable. The same idea operates in the statutory misleading-conduct context under what is now s.18 of the Australian Consumer Law.

No. Hong Kong has no general statutory prohibition on misleading or deceptive conduct in trade or commerce equivalent to s.18 of the Australian Consumer Law (formerly s.52 of the Trade Practices Act 1974). The nearest instruments are sector- or transaction-specific: the Trade Descriptions Ordinance (Cap. 362), as extended by the Trade Descriptions (Unfair Trade Practices) (Amendment) Ordinance 2012, prohibits false trade descriptions, misleading omissions and other unfair trade practices, but it is a criminal statute confined to trader-to-consumer dealings and enforced by Customs and Excise / the Communications Authority rather than creating a general civil cause of action; and the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) provides statutory civil liability for false or misleading inducements in relation to securities and futures (ss.107-108). For general commercial dealings Hong Kong therefore still relies on common law deceit and negligent misstatement plus the Misrepresentation Ordinance (Cap. 284).

There is no such case, and the premise is mistaken. Hong Kong applies the Spiliada test (Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460), received into Hong Kong law in The Adhiguna Meranti [1987] HKLR 904 (CA) and restated by the Court of Final Appeal in SPH v SA (2014) 17 HKCFAR 364: the court asks whether there is another available forum that is clearly or distinctly more appropriate, and if so whether justice nonetheless requires a stay to be refused. That is an evaluative, multifactorial exercise in which connecting factors - governing law, residence of the parties, location of witnesses and evidence, place of the transaction - are weighed qualitatively against each other on the facts. No Hong Kong (or English) authority assigns numerical weights or a fixed tier ranking to individual factors; governing law is usually significant but not decisive, and a plaintiff's residence is generally a weak factor. I would say plainly that no authority exists for the proposition as framed.
